chapters.title: The Blue Carbuncle
paragraphs: On the second morning after Christmas I called on my friend Sherlock Holmes to offer him the greetings of the season. He lay on the sofa in a purple dressing-gown, a rack of pipes within reach on his right. Nearby was a heap of crumpled morning newspapers which he had evidently just read. A wooden chair stood beside the sofa, with a shabby, disreputable hard felt hat hanging from one corner of its back. The hat was badly worn and cracked in several places. A magnifying glass and forceps on the chair’s seat suggested that he had hung it there to examine it.
“You are busy,” I said. “Perhaps I am disturbing you.”

“Not at all. I am glad to have a friend here to discuss my conclusions with. The affair is utterly trivial”—he pointed his thumb towards the old hat—“but certain details are not without interest, and may even teach us something.”

I settled into his armchair and held my hands towards the crackling fire. A hard frost had begun, and ice crystals lay thick on the windows. “I suppose,” I said, “that this ordinary-looking object has some deadly story attached to it: a clue that will help you unravel a mystery and bring a criminal to justice.”

“No, no. There is no crime,” Sherlock Holmes replied, laughing. “Simply one of those curious little incidents inevitable when four million people rub shoulders within a few square miles. In the constant interactions of such a dense mass of humanity, every imaginable combination of events is bound to occur. Many small puzzles arise which can be striking and bizarre without involving crime. We have encountered examples ourselves.”
“Indeed,” I replied. “Of the last six cases I have recorded in my notes, three involved no crime in the legal sense at all.”

“Exactly. You mean my attempt to retrieve the Irene Adler papers, Miss Mary Sutherland’s extraordinary case, and the adventure of the man with the twisted lip. I expect this little affair will prove equally innocent. You know Peterson, the commissionaire?”
“Yes.”
“He is the owner of this trophy.”
“The hat belongs to him?”

“No, no. He found it. We do not know who owns it. Please regard it as a problem for the mind rather than a battered bowler. First, let me explain how it reached me. It arrived on Christmas morning, accompanied by a fine fat goose, which I am sure is now roasting before Peterson’s fire. Here are the facts. At about four on Christmas morning, Peterson—an honest fellow, as you know—was walking home along Tottenham Court Road after a small celebration. Ahead of him, in the gaslight, he saw a rather tall man staggering slightly, with a white goose slung over one shoulder. At the corner of Goodge Street, a quarrel broke out between this stranger and a small group of roughs. One knocked the man’s hat off. He raised his walking stick to defend himself and, swinging it above his head, broke the shop window behind him. Peterson rushed to protect him from his attackers. But the man, alarmed at breaking the glass and seeing an official-looking figure in uniform running towards him, dropped the goose and fled into the maze of narrow streets behind Tottenham Court Road. The roughs had also run off at Peterson’s approach. He therefore found himself master of the battlefield, with the spoils of victory: this battered hat and a Christmas goose of the highest quality.”
“Which he surely returned to their owner?”

“My dear fellow, that is precisely the difficulty. A little card tied to the bird’s left leg did indeed read ‘For Mrs. Henry Baker’, and the initials ‘H. B.’ can be made out inside the hat. But our city contains thousands of Bakers and hundreds of Henry Bakers. Returning lost property to one particular man among them is not easy.”
“What did Peterson do about it?”

“On Christmas morning he brought me both hat and goose, knowing my interest in even the smallest puzzles. We kept the bird until this morning, when it began to show signs that, despite the light frost, it ought to be eaten without further delay. Its finder has therefore taken it away to fulfil a goose’s ultimate destiny. I still have the hat of the unknown gentleman who lost his Christmas dinner.”
“Did he place an advertisement?”
“No.”
“Then what clues can you possibly have to the man’s identity?”
“Only whatever we are able to deduce.”
“From this hat?”
“Exactly.”
“You must be joking. What can this battered old felt tell you?”
“Take my magnifying glass. You know how I work. What can you discover for yourself about the character of the man who wore it?”

I took the ragged object and turned it over without much enthusiasm. It was an ordinary round black hat, stiff and very worn. The lining had once been red silk, but was badly discoloured. There was no maker’s name, though, as Holmes had said, ‘H. B.’ was scrawled on one side. The brim had holes for a hat-securer, but its elastic was gone. Otherwise it was cracked, thick with dust, and stained in several places. Someone seemed to have tried to disguise the discoloured patches by rubbing ink over them.
“I can see nothing in it,” I said, handing it back.
“On the contrary, Watson, everything is there for you to see. What you fail to do is reason from your observations. You draw your conclusions too timidly.”
“Then please explain to me what you can conclude from this hat.”

He took it up and studied it with that inward-looking expression so characteristic of him. “It tells us perhaps less than it might,” he said. “Even so, several conclusions are quite definite, while others are at least strongly probable. Obviously its owner is a man of considerable intellect. He was also fairly prosperous within the last three years, but is now in reduced circumstances. He once thought ahead, though less so now, suggesting a decline in character. Combined with his falling fortunes, that points towards some harmful influence, probably drink, working upon him. This may also explain the obvious fact that his wife no longer loves him.”
“Really, my dear Holmes!”

“He still retains a measure of self-respect, however,” Holmes continued, ignoring my protest. “He is middle-aged, lives a sedentary life, seldom goes out, and is completely out of condition. His hair is greying, has been cut in the last few days, and is treated with lime-cream. These are the more obvious facts his hat reveals. Incidentally, it is also extremely unlikely that his house has gas lighting.”
“Surely you are joking, Holmes.”
“Not in the slightest. Even after I have given you the conclusions, can you still not see how I arrived at them?”
“No doubt I am very stupid, but I admit I cannot follow your reasoning. For instance, how did you decide that the owner was an intellectual man?”

In reply, Holmes put the hat on his head. It slipped over his forehead and came to rest on the bridge of his nose. “A matter of volume,” he said. “A man with a brain that large must have something in it.”
“And his decline in prosperity?”

“The hat is three years old. That was when flat brims with curled edges came into fashion. Its quality is first-rate: notice the ribbed silk band and excellent lining. If he could afford such an expensive hat three years ago, yet has not bought another since, he must certainly have come down in the world.”
“That much is clear enough. But what about his foresight and the decline in his character?”

Sherlock Holmes laughed. “Here is the foresight,” he said, touching the hat-securer’s little disc and loop. “These do not come with a hat. Ordering one shows some capacity to think ahead: he took the extra trouble to protect his hat from the wind. But the elastic has broken, and he has not bothered to replace it. Plainly he is less provident than before, a clear sign of weakening character. On the other hand, he has tried to hide some stains on the felt by covering them with ink. That shows he has not entirely surrendered his self-respect.”
“Your reasoning certainly sounds convincing.”

“The other points—his middle age, his greying hair, its recent cut, and his use of lime-cream—emerge from a close look at the lining’s lower edge. Under the lens we find numerous hair ends, neatly clipped by a barber’s scissors. They seem sticky, and there is a definite smell of lime-cream. Notice, too, the dust: soft and brown, like household dust, rather than the grey grit of the street. This tells us the hat has spent most of its time hanging indoors. The damp marks inside show beyond doubt that its wearer sweats heavily. He can therefore scarcely be in good physical condition.”
“But his wife? You said she no longer loved him.”

“The hat has not been brushed for weeks. My dear Watson, if I see you wearing a hat with a week’s dust on it, and your wife lets you leave home looking like that, I shall fear you too have had the misfortune to lose your wife’s affection.”
“He might be unmarried, though.”
“No. He was taking the goose home as a peace offering to his wife. Remember the card tied to its leg.”
“You can answer everything. But how on earth can you tell that he has no gas supply at home?”

“One stain of candle tallow, or even two, might be accidental. Five suggest strongly that he is often near burning tallow. Most likely he climbs the stairs at night with his hat in one hand and a dripping candle in the other. Whatever the explanation, a gas flame did not leave those tallow marks. Does that satisfy you?”
“It is certainly ingenious,” I said, laughing. “Still, as you have just explained, there is no crime, and the only harm is the loss of a goose. All this effort seems rather wasted.”
Sherlock Holmes was about to answer when the door burst open. Peterson, the commissionaire, hurried into the room, his cheeks flushed and his expression dazed with astonishment.
“The goose, Mr. Holmes! The goose, sir!” he panted.
“Eh? What about it? Has it come back to life and flown out of the kitchen window?” Holmes turned on the sofa to see the man’s excited face more clearly.

“Look, sir! Look what my wife found in its crop!” He stretched out his hand. In the centre of his palm lay a dazzling blue stone, a little smaller than a bean. It was so clear and brilliant that it glittered like a point of electric light in the dark hollow of his hand.
Holmes sat upright and whistled. “By Jove, Peterson! This really is a treasure indeed. I take it you know what you have found?”
“A diamond, sir? Some precious stone. It cuts glass as easily as putty.”
“More than a precious stone. It is _the_ precious stone.”
“Surely not the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle!” I exclaimed.

“Exactly. I should recognise its size and shape: lately I have read the advertisement in _The Times_ every day. It is unique, and its value can only be guessed. The thousand-pound reward offered is certainly less than one twentieth of what it would fetch on the market.”
“A thousand pounds! Great Lord of mercy!” The commissionaire collapsed into a chair and stared back and forth between us.
“That is the reward. I also have reason to know that sentimental matters are involved, which would persuade the Countess to surrender half her fortune merely to get the jewel back.”
“If I remember correctly, it disappeared at the Hotel Cosmopolitan,” I said.

“Yes, on December twenty-second, exactly five days ago. A plumber, John Horner, was accused of taking it from the Countess’s jewel-case. The evidence seemed so strong that he has been sent for trial at the Assizes. I believe I have a report here.” He searched among the newspapers, checking their dates, until he found one, smoothed it out, folded it over, and read this paragraph:

“Jewel Robbery at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. John Horner, a plumber aged twenty-six, appeared charged with stealing the valuable blue carbuncle from the Countess of Morcar’s jewel-case on the twenty-second of this month. James Ryder, the hotel’s senior attendant, testified that on the day of the theft he took Horner to the Countess’s dressing-room to solder the second bar of the grate, which had worked loose. He stayed with Horner for a short time, but was then called away. Returning, he found Horner gone, the bureau forced open, and a small morocco-leather casket lying empty on the dressing-table. It was later established that the Countess kept her jewel in this box. Ryder raised the alarm immediately. Horner was arrested that evening, but neither a search of his person nor of his rooms revealed the stone. Catherine Cusack, the Countess’s maid, stated that she heard Ryder cry out on discovering the theft. She rushed into the room and found it as he had described. Inspector Bradstreet of B Division testified about Horner’s arrest. The accused struggled violently and protested his innocence in the strongest language. After hearing evidence of the prisoner’s previous conviction for robbery, the magistrate declined to deal with the offence summarily and committed it to the Assizes. Horner, who had been visibly distressed throughout the hearing, fainted at its conclusion and was carried from the court.”

“Hmm! That settles what happened in the police-court,” Holmes said thoughtfully, tossing the paper aside. “Our task is to trace the events connecting a plundered jewel-case at one end with a goose’s crop in Tottenham Court Road at the other. You see, Watson, our little deductions have suddenly become much more serious and far less innocent. Here is the stone. It came from the goose, and the goose came from Henry Baker, the owner of the shabby hat and all those other characteristics with which I have bored you. We must now make a serious effort to find him and discover his part in the mystery. Let us begin with the simplest method: advertisements in all the evening newspapers. If that fails, I have other methods to turn to.”
“How will you word it?”

“Hand me a pencil and that piece of paper. Now: ‘Found at the corner of Goodge Street: a goose and a black felt hat. Mr. Henry Baker may reclaim them at 6:30 this evening, at 221B Baker Street.’ Clear and brief.”
“Very. But is he likely to see it?”

“He is bound to watch the newspapers: for a man without much money, this was a serious loss. Breaking the window and seeing Peterson approach evidently frightened him into thinking of nothing but escape. Since then, he must have bitterly regretted the impulse that made him abandon his bird. Besides, including his name will help bring the notice to him, since everyone who knows him will point it out. Here, Peterson: take this to the advertising agency and have it placed in the evening papers.”
“Which ones, sir?”
“Oh, the _Globe_, _Star_, _Pall Mall_, _St. James’s Gazette_, _Evening News_, _Standard_, _Echo_, and any others you can think of.”
“Very good, sir. What about the stone?”
“Ah, yes, I will keep that. Thank you. And Peterson, buy another goose on your way back and bring it here. We must give this gentleman a replacement for the one your family is now eating.”

After the commissionaire left, Holmes picked up the jewel and held it to the light. “A beautiful thing,” he said. “Look how it flashes and sparkles. Naturally it is a centre of criminal activity. Every fine jewel is. They are the devil’s favourite lures. In a large, ancient gem, each facet may represent some bloody deed. This one is not yet twenty years old. It was discovered in the banks of the Amoy River in southern China, and has all the properties of a carbuncle except its colour: blue instead of ruby red. Young as it is, it already has a sinister past. Two murders, an acid attack, a suicide, and several robberies have been committed for this forty-grain piece of crystallised charcoal. Who would imagine such a pretty plaything could supply victims for prison and the gallows? I shall put it in my strongbox now and write to the Countess to tell her we have it.”
“Do you believe this man Horner is innocent?”
“I cannot say.”
“Then do you suspect the other man, Henry Baker, of having some connection with the affair?”

“I consider it much more likely that Henry Baker is entirely innocent. He probably had no idea that his goose was worth considerably more than if the whole bird had been made of solid gold. If our advertisement produces a reply, however, a very simple test will settle that question.”
“And until then there is nothing you can do?”
“Nothing.”
“Then I shall resume my medical rounds. But I will return this evening at the time you named. I want to see how you untangle such a complicated affair.”
“I shall be glad to see you. Dinner is at seven; I believe we have woodcock. Incidentally, after what has happened, perhaps I should ask Mrs. Hudson to inspect its crop.”

A patient delayed me, and it was a little past half-past six when I returned to Baker Street. As I approached the house, I saw a tall man waiting in the bright semicircle of light cast by the fanlight. He wore a Scottish bonnet and a coat fastened to his chin. The door opened just as I arrived, and we were shown upstairs to Holmes together.

“Mr. Henry Baker, I take it,” Holmes said, rising from his armchair and welcoming the visitor with the effortless cordiality he could so readily adopt. “Please sit by the fire, Mr. Baker. The night is cold, and I notice your circulation suits summer better than winter. Ah, Watson, you are just in time. Is this your hat, Mr. Baker?”
“Yes, sir. That is certainly my hat.”

He was a large, round-shouldered man with a massive head and a broad, intelligent face tapering towards a pointed beard of brown streaked with grey. His reddish nose and cheeks, and the slight trembling of his outstretched hand, recalled Holmes’s guess about his habits. His faded black frock-coat was buttoned to the top, its collar turned up. Thin wrists extended from the sleeves without any shirt or cuffs showing. He spoke slowly, in short bursts, choosing each word carefully. Altogether he suggested an educated, literary man who had been treated badly by fortune.
“We kept these things for several days,” Holmes said, “expecting you to advertise with your address. I must admit I do not understand why you failed to do so.”

The visitor laughed rather sheepishly. “Shillings are less plentiful with me than they used to be,” he said. “I was certain the roughs who attacked me had taken both the goose and my hat. I did not wish to waste more money on a hopeless attempt to retrieve them.”
“Quite understandable. As for the bird, I am afraid we had to eat it.”
“Eat it!” In his agitation, our visitor half rose from his chair.
“Yes. Otherwise it would have been no use to anybody. But I imagine this other goose on the sideboard will serve you just as well. It is quite fresh and roughly the same weight.”
“Oh, certainly, certainly,” Mr. Baker replied, sighing with relief.
“Naturally we still have your own bird’s feathers, legs, crop, and so forth. If you would like them—”

The man laughed heartily. “They might serve as mementoes of my adventure,” he said. “Beyond that, I can scarcely imagine what use the _disjecta membra_ of my departed acquaintance would be to me. No, sir. With your permission, I shall direct my attention solely to the excellent bird I see on your sideboard.”
Sherlock Holmes gave me a sharp glance and a small shrug of his shoulders.

“Then here is your hat, and here is your goose,” he said. “Incidentally, would you mind telling me where you obtained the original bird? I take an interest in poultry and have rarely seen such a well-grown goose.”

“Of course, sir,” said Baker, rising and tucking his newly acquired property under his arm. “Several of us regularly visit the Alpha Inn near the Museum. During the day, you understand, you will find us at the Museum itself. This year our excellent landlord, Windigate, started a goose club. By paying a few pence each week, each member was entitled to a bird at Christmas. I paid my contributions, and you know what followed. I am most grateful to you, sir: a Scottish bonnet suits neither my age nor my dignity.” With an amusingly pompous air, he bowed solemnly to us both and strode away.
“That settles Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes after the door closed behind him. “Clearly he knows absolutely nothing of this affair. Are you hungry, Watson?”
“Not especially.”
“Then let us make a late supper of our dinner and pursue this clue while it is still fresh.”
“Certainly, let us.”

The night was bitterly cold. We put on our heavy ulster coats and wound cravats around our necks. Outside, stars shone coldly from a cloudless sky, and each passer-by’s breath burst into vapour like smoke from a pistol. Our steps rang sharp and loud as we strode through the doctors’ district—Wimpole Street, Harley Street, then Wigmore Street and Oxford Street. Fifteen minutes brought us to the Alpha Inn in Bloomsbury, a small public-house on the corner of a street leading into Holborn. Holmes opened the private bar’s door and asked the red-faced landlord in his white apron for two glasses of beer.
“If your beer matches your geese,” he said, “it should be excellent.”
“My geese!” The landlord looked startled.
“Yes. Only half an hour ago I was speaking with Henry Baker, one of your goose-club members.”
“Ah, yes, I see. But they aren’t _our_ geese, sir.”
“Really! Whose are they, then?”
“I bought the two dozen from a dealer at Covent Garden.”
“Indeed? I know a few dealers there. Which one?”
“His name is Breckinridge.”
“Ah! I do not know him. Well, your good health, landlord, and success to your establishment. Good night.”

“Now to find Mr. Breckinridge,” Holmes said, fastening his coat as we stepped into the frosty air. “Remember, Watson: at one end of this chain is an ordinary goose. At the other stands a man certain to receive seven years’ penal servitude unless we can prove him innocent. Our enquiries may only establish his guilt more firmly. Either way, a remarkable accident has given us a path to follow which the police have overlooked. We must pursue it to the very end. Face south, then, and quick march!”

We crossed Holborn, went down Endell Street, and wound through a series of slums to Covent Garden Market. Breckinridge’s name appeared above one of the largest stalls. Its owner, a sharp-faced man with neat side-whiskers and the look of a racing enthusiast, was helping a boy put up the shutters.
“Good evening. A cold night,” Holmes remarked.
The dealer nodded, casting a questioning look at my companion.
“I see you have no geese left,” Holmes continued, indicating the empty marble slabs.
“Could supply you five hundred tomorrow morning.”
“That will not do.”
“Then try the stall over there with the gas flare.”
“Ah, but someone specifically recommended you.”
“Who was that?”
“The landlord at the Alpha.”
“Oh, yes. I supplied him with two dozen.”
“Excellent birds, too. Where did you buy them, if I may ask?”
To my surprise, this question made the dealer burst into anger.
“Now look here, mister,” he said, head tilted and hands on hips. “What are you getting at? Come out with it.”
“I have been quite direct. I want to know who supplied the geese you sold to the Alpha.”
“Well, I won’t tell you. There you are!”
“It hardly matters, but I cannot see why such a small question should make you so angry.”

“Angry! You might be angry too if people pestered you as they do me. I pay good money for good goods, and that ought to finish the business. Instead it’s ‘Where are the geese?’ and ‘Who bought the geese?’ and ‘How much do you want for the geese?’ Hearing all this fuss, you’d think no other geese existed in the world.”

“I have nothing to do with anyone else who has been asking,” Holmes said casually. “If you refuse to tell us, we must cancel the bet, that is all. I am always willing to back my judgement about poultry, though. I have five pounds riding on that bird having been reared in the country.”
“Then you’ve lost your five pounds. It was reared in town,” the dealer snapped.
“It certainly was not.”
“I tell you it was.”
“I do not believe you.”
“Think you know more about poultry than a man who’s handled it since he was a little boy? I’m telling you, every bird I sent to the Alpha was town-bred.”
“Nothing you say will convince me of that.”
“Will you bet on it?”
“That would simply be taking your money, since I know I am right. Still, I will wager a sovereign, just to teach you not to be so stubborn.”
The dealer gave a grim chuckle. “Fetch the books, Bill,” he said.
The boy brought a small, thin book and a large one with a greasy cover, placing them together under the hanging lamp.
“Now, Mr. Know-it-all,” the dealer said, “I thought I’d run out of geese, but before we’re finished you’ll find one still left in my shop. See this little book?”
“Well, what of it?”

“It lists the people I buy from. Understand? This page has the country suppliers, and the numbers after their names tell you where their accounts are in the big ledger. Now look at the other page, written in red. Those are my town suppliers. See the third name? Read it aloud for me.”
“Mrs. Oakshott, 117 Brixton Road—249,” Holmes read aloud.
“Exactly. Now find that page in the ledger.”
Holmes opened the ledger at the indicated page. “Here it is: ‘Mrs. Oakshott, 117 Brixton Road, supplier of eggs and poultry.’”
“Now read out the final entry.”
“‘December twenty-second. Twenty-four geese at seven shillings and sixpence.’”
“Right. There’s your answer. And below that?”
“‘Sold to Mr. Windigate at the Alpha for twelve shillings.’”
“What do you say to that?”

Holmes looked thoroughly crestfallen. He took a sovereign from his pocket, tossed it onto the marble, and turned away as though too disgusted to speak. A few yards farther on, he stopped beneath a street lamp and laughed with that hearty, silent amusement peculiar to him.

“A man with whiskers like those and the ‘Pink ’un’ sticking out of his pocket can always be drawn into a wager,” he said. “I doubt that putting a hundred pounds down in front of him would have produced such full information as the thought of beating me at a bet. Well, Watson, I think our search is nearly over. The only question we still need to decide is whether to visit Mrs. Oakshott tonight or leave it until tomorrow. That surly fellow’s remarks make it plain that other people besides ourselves are taking an anxious interest in the affair. I should—”

His words were suddenly interrupted by a loud disturbance from the stall we had just left. Turning, we saw a small, rat-faced man standing in the centre of the yellow circle of light cast by the swinging lamp. Breckinridge stood framed in the stall doorway, shaking his fists furiously at the cowering figure.

“I’ve had enough of you and your geese!” he shouted. “The devil take the lot of you! Bother me again with your nonsense and I’ll put the dog on you. Bring Mrs. Oakshott here and I’ll answer her. But what business is it of yours? Did I buy them from you?”
“No, but one of them belonged to me all the same,” the little man whined.
“Then go and ask Mrs. Oakshott for it.”
“She sent me to ask you.”
“Ask the King of Proosia, for all I care. I’ve had enough. Get out!” He charged forward angrily, and the questioner darted away into the dark.

“Ah! This may spare us the journey to Brixton Road,” Holmes whispered. “Come along. Let us see what we can learn from him.” He strode through the scattered groups lingering beside the brightly lit stalls, quickly caught the little man, and touched his shoulder. The man spun round. By the gaslight I could see that every trace of colour had drained from his face.
“Who are you? What do you want with me?” he asked, his voice trembling.
“Forgive me,” Holmes said pleasantly. “I could not avoid hearing the questions you just asked that dealer. I believe I may be able to help you.”
“You? Who are you? How could you know anything about it?”
“I am Sherlock Holmes. Knowing what other people do not know is my profession.”
“But surely you cannot know anything about this?”

“On the contrary, I know the whole affair. You are tracing geese sold by Mrs. Oakshott of Brixton Road to a dealer called Breckinridge. He sold them to Mr. Windigate at the Alpha, who distributed them to his club, which includes Mr. Henry Baker.”
“Oh, sir, you are exactly the man I have wanted to find!” cried the little fellow, reaching out with trembling fingers. “I can hardly tell you how much this matter means to me.”

Holmes hailed a passing four-wheeled cab. “Then let us discuss it in a comfortable room instead of this windswept market,” he said. “Before we go any further, though, please tell me whom I have the pleasure of helping.”
The man paused briefly. “My name is John Robinson,” he replied, with a sideways look.
“No, no. Your true name,” Holmes said gently. “Conducting business under an assumed name is always inconvenient.”
Colour flooded the stranger’s pale cheeks. “Very well,” he said. “My real name is James Ryder.”
“Exactly. The senior attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. Please get into the cab. I shall soon be able to tell you everything you want to know.”

The little man looked from one of us to the other, half afraid and half hopeful, like someone unsure whether good fortune or disaster awaited him. Then he climbed into the cab. Half an hour later we were in the Baker Street sitting-room. Nobody spoke during the journey, but our new companion’s thin, rapid breathing and the constant clenching and unclenching of his hands betrayed his nervous strain.

“Here we are!” Holmes said cheerfully as we entered. “A fire is very welcome in weather like this. You look cold, Mr. Ryder. Take the wicker chair. I shall put on my slippers, then we can settle your little difficulty. Now! You want to learn what happened to those geese?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Or rather to one goose, I imagine. Surely one particular bird concerned you: a white one with a black bar across its tail.”
Ryder trembled with excitement. “Oh, sir!” he cried. “Can you tell me where it ended up?”
“It ended up here.”
“Here, you say?”
“Yes, and a remarkable bird it was. No wonder it interested you. After it died, it laid an egg: the prettiest, brightest little blue egg anyone ever saw. I have it here in my collection.”

Our visitor lurched to his feet and gripped the mantelpiece with his right hand. Holmes unlocked his strongbox and raised the blue carbuncle. It shone like a star, sending out cold, brilliant rays in every direction. Ryder stared, his face strained, unable to decide whether to claim the stone or deny it.

“You are found out, Ryder,” Holmes said quietly. “Steady yourself, man, or you will fall into the fire! Help him back to his chair, Watson. He has not the nerve to commit a felony and get away with it. Give him a little brandy. There! He looks more human now. What a feeble little creature!”
For a moment Ryder had swayed and almost fallen. The brandy restored a little colour to his cheeks, and he sat gazing fearfully at the man who accused him.

“I have almost the entire chain of events, and all the evidence I could need. There is very little left for you to tell me. We may as well settle those few details, though, and complete the case. You had heard of the Countess of Morcar’s blue jewel, Ryder?”
“It was Catherine Cusack who told me about it,” he answered, his voice cracking.

“I see. Her ladyship’s maid. The prospect of sudden wealth, so easily gained, proved too tempting—as it has for better men before you. But you showed few scruples about your methods. Ryder, I think you have the makings of a very accomplished villain. You knew Horner the plumber had been involved in a similar affair before, so suspicion would readily fall on him. What did you do? You and your accomplice Cusack arranged a small repair in the Countess’s room, then made sure Horner was called to do it. After he left, you emptied the jewel-case, raised the alarm, and had the unfortunate man arrested. Then you—”

Ryder suddenly flung himself onto the rug and grasped Holmes’s knees. “For God’s sake, show mercy!” he shrieked. “Think of my father and mother! It would break their hearts. I have never done wrong before! I never will again. I swear it—I’ll swear on the Bible. Oh, do not take it to court! For Christ’s sake, don’t!”
“Back into your chair!” Holmes ordered sternly. “It is easy enough to crawl and beg now. You showed little concern for poor Horner, standing trial for a crime he knew nothing about.”
“I will run away, Mr. Holmes. I will leave the country. Then the case against him will fall apart.”

“Hmm! We shall discuss that. First, give us a truthful account of what happened next. How did the stone get inside the goose, and how did the goose reach the market? Your only chance of safety lies in telling us the truth.”

Ryder ran his tongue over his parched lips. “I will tell you exactly what happened, sir. After Horner’s arrest, I decided I should leave with the jewel immediately. At any moment the police might think of searching me or my room. There was nowhere in the hotel where I could safely hide it. I went out as though on an errand and headed for my sister’s house. She had married a man called Oakshott and lived in Brixton Road, where she fattened poultry for sale. Every man I passed seemed to be a policeman or detective. Cold as the night was, sweat was running down my face before I reached Brixton Road. My sister asked what was wrong and why I looked so pale. I told her the jewel robbery at the hotel had upset me. Then I went into the backyard where I smoked a pipe and tried to decide what would be best to do next.

“I once had a friend named Maudsley who turned criminal and has lately been serving a sentence in Pentonville. One day when we met, he talked about thieves and how they disposed of stolen goods. I knew he would keep faith with me, because I knew a thing or two about him. I decided to go straight to his home in Kilburn and confide in him. He could tell me how to turn the jewel into cash. But how could I reach him safely? I remembered the torment of my journey from the hotel. At any moment I might be stopped and searched, and there would be the stone in my waistcoat pocket. I was leaning against the wall, watching geese waddle around my feet, when an idea suddenly occurred to me. It showed me how to outwit the finest detective who ever lived.

“Some weeks earlier my sister had promised me my choice of her geese as a Christmas present. She always kept her promises. I would collect my goose now and use it to carry the jewel to Kilburn. A small shed stood in the yard. I drove one bird behind it, a fine big white goose with a barred tail. I caught it, forced its bill open, and pushed the stone as far down its throat as my finger would go. It gulped, and I felt the stone move along its gullet into its crop. But it struggled and flapped, bringing my sister out to investigate. When I turned to speak to her, the creature escaped and fluttered back among the other birds.
“‘What on earth were you doing to that goose, Jem?’ she asked.
“‘Well,’ I said, ‘you promised me one for Christmas. I was feeling them to find the fattest.’
“‘Oh,’ she said, ‘we’ve already put yours aside. We call it Jem’s bird. That big white one over there. There are twenty-six altogether: one for you, one for us, and two dozen to sell.’
“‘Thank you, Maggie,’ I said. ‘But if you don’t mind, I would rather take the one I was just holding.’
“‘The other weighs a good three pounds more,’ she said. ‘We fattened it especially for you.’
“‘Never mind. I want the other one, and I’ll take it now,’ I replied.
“‘Oh, please yourself,’ she said, a little offended. ‘Which one do you want, then?’
“‘The white one with the barred tail, there in the middle of the flock.’
“‘Very well. Kill it and take it away with you.’

“I did as she said, Mr. Holmes, and carried the goose all the way to Kilburn. I told my friend what I had done. He was the kind of man one could easily tell such a thing to. He laughed until he nearly choked. Then we took a knife and opened the bird. My heart sank: the jewel was not there. I knew I had made some terrible mistake. Leaving the goose, I rushed back to my sister’s and into the backyard. Not a single bird remained.
“‘Where have they all gone, Maggie?’ I cried.
“‘To the dealer, Jem.’
“‘To which dealer?’
“‘Breckinridge at Covent Garden.’
“‘Was there another goose with a barred tail?’ I asked. ‘Just like the one I took?’
“‘Yes, Jem. Two of them had barred tails, and I could never tell which was which.’

“Then I understood everything. I ran as fast as I could to Breckinridge, but he had sold the whole lot immediately and would not say a word about where they had gone. You heard him tonight. That is how he has answered me every time. My sister thinks I am losing my mind. Sometimes I think so myself. And now—now I am branded a thief, without ever enjoying the wealth for which I sold my good name. God help me! God help me!” Burying his face in his hands, he broke into violent sobs.
A long silence followed. Only Ryder’s heavy breathing and the steady tapping of Holmes’s fingertips on the table’s edge disturbed it. At last my friend stood and flung the door open.
“Leave!” he said.
“What, sir! Oh, may Heaven bless you!”
“Not another word. Get out!”
He needed no further encouragement. There was a sudden rush, clattering feet on the staircase, a door slammed, and then the sharp sound of running footsteps outside.

“After all, Watson,” Holmes said, reaching for his clay pipe, “the police do not employ me to make up for their shortcomings. If Horner were still in danger, that would be different. But this man will not testify against him, and the prosecution must fail. I suppose I am commuting a felony, but perhaps I am saving a soul. He will not stray again: he is far too frightened. Put him in prison now and you make him a prison-bird for life. Besides, this is the season for forgiveness. Chance offered us an extraordinary, fanciful puzzle; solving it is reward enough. Ring the bell, if you please, Doctor, and we can begin another investigation in which a bird will also play the leading part.”

chapters.title: The Speckled Band
paragraphs: Looking through my notes on the seventy-odd cases in which I have watched Sherlock Holmes’s methods over the past eight years, I find much that is tragic, some that is comic, and a great deal that is simply strange. None is commonplace. My friend worked for love of his art rather than money, and refused investigations unless they promised something unusual, even fantastic. Yet among all these varied affairs, I cannot remember one with stranger features than the case involving the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, that well-known Surrey family. It took place early in my friendship with Holmes, when we were both bachelors sharing rooms in Baker Street. I might have recorded it sooner, but at the time I promised secrecy. Only last month did the premature death of the woman to whom I gave that promise release me from it. Perhaps it is just as well to make the facts public now. I have reason to know that rumours about the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott are widespread, and make the affair sound even more dreadful than it really was.

Early one morning in April 1883, I woke to find Sherlock Holmes standing fully dressed beside my bed. As a rule he rose rather late. Seeing from the mantelpiece clock that it was only a quarter past seven, I blinked up at him in surprise and perhaps with a little resentment, for my own habits were regular.
“Sorry to wake you, Watson,” he said, “but we are all suffering alike this morning. Someone woke Mrs. Hudson, she passed the favour on to me, and I to you.”
“What has happened? Is there a fire?”

“No, a client. A young woman has apparently arrived in a state of great agitation and insists on seeing me. She is waiting in the sitting-room. When young women roam London at this hour, waking people from their beds, I assume they have something urgent to tell us. If the case proves interesting, I am sure you would want to follow it from the beginning. At any rate, I thought I should wake you and offer you the chance.”
“My dear fellow, nothing would make me miss it.”

Nothing delighted me more than accompanying Holmes on his professional enquiries and admiring the swift deductions with which he solved the problems brought to him. They were as quick as intuition, yet always grounded in logic. I hurried into my clothes and within minutes was ready to follow him downstairs. A heavily veiled woman dressed in black had been sitting by the window. She stood as we entered.

“Good morning, madam,” Holmes said cheerfully. “I am Sherlock Holmes. This is my close friend and colleague, Dr. Watson. You may speak before him as freely as before me. Ah! I am pleased Mrs. Hudson has sensibly lit the fire. Please move closer to it. I shall ask for some hot coffee, since I can see you are shivering.”
“It is not the cold that makes me tremble,” she said quietly, moving her chair as he suggested.
“What is it, then?”

“Fear, Mr. Holmes. Terror.” As she lifted her veil, we saw that she was indeed pitifully distressed. Her face was drawn and grey, her frightened eyes restless like those of a hunted animal. Her face and figure suggested a woman of thirty, but her hair was prematurely streaked with grey, and she looked weary and haggard. Holmes surveyed her with one of his quick glances that seemed to take in everything.
“Do not be afraid,” he said gently, leaning forward and patting her forearm. “I am sure we can soon put things right. I see you travelled here by train this morning.”
“Then you know who I am?”

“No, but I see the unused half of a return ticket in the palm of your left glove. You must have set out early, yet before reaching the station you had a considerable drive in a dog-cart over muddy roads.”
The woman started sharply and stared at Holmes in bewilderment.

“There is nothing mysterious about it, madam,” he said, smiling. “Your jacket’s left sleeve has no fewer than seven splashes of mud, all perfectly fresh. Only a dog-cart throws mud in that particular way, and only when its passenger sits to the driver’s left.”

“Whatever your reasoning, you are entirely right,” she said. “I left home before six, reached Leatherhead at twenty past, and caught the first train to Waterloo. Sir, I cannot bear this strain any longer. If it continues, I shall go mad. There is nobody to turn to—only one person who cares for me, and he, poor man, can do little. I have heard about you, Mr. Holmes, from Mrs. Farintosh, whom you helped when she was in desperate need. She gave me your address. Oh, sir, could you not help me too, and cast at least a little light into the darkness around me? I cannot pay for your services now. But I shall be married in a month or six weeks, with control over my own income. Then you will certainly not find me ungrateful.”
Holmes went to his desk, unlocked it, and took out a small case-book, which he opened and consulted.

“Farintosh,” he said. “Ah, yes, I remember the case. It involved an opal tiara, and I think it was before your time, Watson. Madam, I can only assure you that I shall gladly give your case the same care and attention I gave your friend’s. As for payment, my work is its own reward. You may cover whatever expenses I incur at whichever time is most convenient for you. Now please set before us everything that might help us form an opinion about this affair.”

“Alas!” our visitor answered. “The worst of it is that my fears are so indefinite. My suspicions rest on tiny details that might seem unimportant to anyone else. Even the person I have most right to turn to for help and advice thinks everything I tell him is merely a nervous woman’s imagination. He does not say so, but I see it in his soothing replies and the way he avoids my eyes. I have heard, Mr. Holmes, that you understand the many forms of wickedness in the human heart. Perhaps you can tell me how to make my way through the dangers surrounding me.”
“You have my full attention, madam.”
“My name is Helen Stoner. I live with my stepfather, the last surviving member of one of England’s oldest Saxon families: the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, on Surrey’s western boundary.”
Holmes nodded. “I am familiar with the name,” he said.

“The family was once among England’s wealthiest. Its estates stretched north into Berkshire and west into Hampshire. During the last century, however, four successive heirs lived recklessly and squandered their fortunes. A gambler in the Regency period finally completed the ruin. Only a few acres remained, with the two-hundred-year-old house, itself burdened by a heavy mortgage. The last squire lingered there, living out the long, miserable existence of an aristocratic pauper. His only son, my stepfather, recognised that he must adapt to changed circumstances. A relative advanced him money for a medical degree, and he went to Calcutta. His professional ability and force of character soon built him a large practice. Then, enraged by robberies at his house, he beat his native butler to death. He narrowly escaped a death sentence. Instead, he spent many years in prison and returned to England a deeply bitter, disappointed man.

“While in India, Dr. Roylott married my mother, Mrs. Stoner, the young widow of Major-General Stoner of the Bengal Artillery. My twin sister Julia and I were only two when she remarried. Mother had a substantial income, at least a thousand pounds a year. She left all of it to Dr. Roylott while we lived with him, but stipulated that each of us should receive a certain yearly sum if we married. Soon after we returned to England, she died: she was killed in a railway accident near Crewe eight years ago. Dr. Roylott then gave up trying to establish a London practice and took us to the old family house at Stoke Moran. Mother’s money provided everything we needed, and there seemed no reason we should not be happy.

“But at about that time our stepfather changed terribly. The neighbours were initially delighted to see a Roylott back in the ancestral home. Instead of making friends and exchanging visits, however, he shut himself inside, emerging mainly to quarrel savagely with anyone he encountered. A violent temper bordering on madness has run through the family’s men for generations. In my stepfather, I believe, his long years in the tropics made it worse. A series of shameful brawls followed, two ending in the police-court. Eventually he became the terror of the village. People ran from him when he approached: he is immensely strong, and once angry is utterly beyond control.

“Last week he threw the village blacksmith over a parapet into a stream. Only by handing over every penny I could gather did I prevent another public scandal. He has no friends except the wandering gipsies. He lets these vagabonds camp on the few bramble-covered acres left of the estate, and in exchange enjoys their hospitality in their tents. Sometimes he wanders off with them for weeks. He also loves Indian animals, which a correspondent sends him. At present he keeps a cheetah and a baboon roaming freely through the grounds. The villagers fear them almost as much as they fear their master.

“You can imagine how little pleasure my poor sister Julia and I had in such a life. No servant would remain, and for a long time we did all the housework ourselves. She was only thirty when she died, yet her hair had already started to turn white, as mine has.”
“Then your sister has died?”

“Exactly two years ago. Her death is what I want to discuss. With the life I have described, we rarely met anyone of our own age and social position. We did, however, have an aunt—our mother’s unmarried sister, Miss Honoria Westphail—who lives near Harrow. Sometimes we were permitted short visits to her. Julia went there at Christmas two years ago and met a major of marines on half-pay. They became engaged. On her return, she told my stepfather, who raised no objection. But within two weeks of the date fixed for their wedding, the dreadful event occurred that robbed me of my only companion.”
Sherlock Holmes had been leaning back, eyes closed and head resting on a cushion. Now he half opened his eyes and looked towards our visitor.
“Please give the details precisely,” he said.

“That is easy: every incident of that dreadful time is burned into my memory. As I said, the manor-house is ancient, and only one wing is occupied now. Its bedrooms are on the ground floor, while the sitting-rooms are in the central block. The first bedroom belongs to Dr. Roylott, the second was my sister’s, and the third is mine. No doors connect the rooms, but each opens onto the same corridor. Is that clear?”
“Completely clear.”

“All three windows face the lawn. On that fatal night, Dr. Roylott went to his room early. We knew he had not gone to sleep, because my sister was bothered by the smell of the strong Indian cigars he smoked. She came into my room instead and stayed for some time, talking about her approaching wedding. At eleven she got up to go, but paused in the doorway and looked back.
“‘Helen,’ she said, ‘have you ever heard someone whistling in the middle of the night?’
“‘Not once,’ I replied.
“‘Could you perhaps be whistling yourself while you are asleep?’
“‘Certainly not. Why do you ask?’

“‘For the last few nights, at about three in the morning, I have heard a low, clear whistle. I sleep lightly, and it wakes me. I cannot tell whether it comes from the next room or perhaps from the lawn. I thought I would ask if you had heard it too.’
“‘No, I haven’t. It must be those wretched gipsies camped in the plantation.’
“‘Probably. Still, if it comes from the lawn, I wonder why you do not hear it.’
“‘But I sleep more soundly than you do.’
“‘Well, it cannot matter very much.’ She smiled at me, closed my door, and a few moments later I heard the key turn in her own lock.”
“Indeed,” Holmes said. “Did you always lock your bedroom doors at night?”
“Every night.”
“Why was that?”
“I believe I already mentioned that the Doctor keeps a cheetah and a baboon. We never felt safe unless we had locked ourselves in.”
“Of course. Please continue your account.”

“I could not sleep. An uneasy sense of approaching disaster troubled me. Remember, we were twins, and you know how subtle the bonds can be between two souls so closely connected. It was a wild night: wind howled outside and rain beat and splashed against the windows. Suddenly, through the storm’s uproar, came a woman’s wild scream of terror. I recognised my sister’s voice. I jumped from bed, wrapped a shawl around myself, and ran into the corridor. As I opened my door, I thought I heard the low whistle she had described. Moments later came a clang, as though something heavy and metal had fallen. I hurried down the passage. My sister’s door was unlocked and swinging slowly open. I stared at it in horror, unable to imagine what might emerge. In the corridor lamp’s light she appeared in the doorway, her face white with terror, her hands reaching for help. Her whole body swayed like a drunkard’s. I ran to her and put my arms around her, but her knees gave way and she collapsed. She writhed in terrible pain, her limbs seized by dreadful convulsions. At first I thought she did not recognise me. Then, as I bent over her, she suddenly screamed in a voice I can never forget, ‘Oh, my God! Helen! It was the band! The speckled band!’ She wanted to say more and jabbed a finger towards the Doctor’s room, but another convulsion cut off her words. I rushed away, calling for my stepfather, and met him hurrying from his room in his dressing-gown. By the time he reached her, she was unconscious. He poured brandy down her throat and sent to the village for medical help, but nothing could save her. She slowly weakened and died without regaining consciousness. That was my beloved sister’s dreadful end.”
“A moment,” Holmes said. “Are you certain about the whistle and the metallic noise? Could you swear you heard them?”
“The county coroner asked me that at the inquest. I strongly believe I heard them. Yet with the storm crashing outside and the old house creaking, it is possible I was mistaken.”
“Was she fully dressed?”
“No, she wore her nightdress. They found a burnt match end in her right hand and a matchbox in her left.”
“Which shows that she lit a match and looked around when something alarmed her. That matters. What conclusion did the coroner reach?”

“He examined everything with great care, since Dr. Roylott’s behaviour had long been notorious throughout the county. But he could find no satisfactory explanation for her death. My testimony established that the door was locked from inside. Old-fashioned shutters with broad iron bars covered the windows and were secured every night. The walls were sounded carefully and proved solid all around. The floor was thoroughly inspected with the same result. The chimney is wide, but four large staples block it. My sister must therefore have been entirely alone when she died. Nor did her body show any signs of violence.”
“What about poison?”
“The doctors looked for evidence of that, but found none.”
“What, then, do you believe caused this unfortunate woman’s death?”
“I believe sheer terror and nervous shock killed her. But I cannot imagine what could have frightened her so much.”
“Were any gipsies camping in the plantation then?”
“Yes. Some are almost always there.”
“Ah. What did you make of her reference to a band—a speckled band?”

“Sometimes I think it was merely delirium. At other times I wonder if she meant a group of people, perhaps those gipsies in the plantation. Many of them wear spotted handkerchiefs on their heads. I cannot say whether that might explain the strange adjective she chose.”
Holmes shook his head with the air of a man far from satisfied.
“These are deep waters indeed,” he said. “Please continue with your story.”

“Two years have gone by, and until recently my life has been lonelier than ever. A month ago, however, a dear friend of many years honoured me by proposing marriage. His name is Armitage—Percy Armitage—the second son of Mr. Armitage of Crane Water, near Reading. My stepfather has not opposed the match, and we intend to marry this spring. Two days ago repairs began on the west wing. They have made a hole in my bedroom wall, forcing me to move into the room where my sister died and sleep in her very bed. Imagine my terror last night when, lying awake and thinking of her dreadful fate, I suddenly heard that same low whistle through the silence—the sound that had preceded her death. I leaped up and lit the lamp, but could see nothing in the room. Too frightened to return to bed, I dressed. At the first daylight I slipped downstairs, hired a dog-cart at the Crown Inn opposite, and drove to Leatherhead. From there I came straight here this morning, solely to see you and ask your advice.”
“You were right to come,” my friend said. “But have you told me everything?”
“Yes, everything.”
“Miss Roylott, you have not. You are protecting your stepfather.”
“What do you mean by that?”
Instead of answering, Holmes drew back the black lace frill edging the hand that rested on our visitor’s knee. Five small, livid marks—four fingers and a thumb—stood out on her white wrist.
“Someone has treated you cruelly,” Holmes said.
She blushed deeply and covered her injured wrist. “He is a harsh man,” she said. “Perhaps he does not realise how strong he is.”
For a long while nobody spoke. Holmes rested his chin on his hands and gazed into the crackling fire.

“This is a very complex affair,” he said at last. “There are a thousand separate details I should like to learn before deciding what to do. Yet we cannot spare a moment. If we came to Stoke Moran today, could we inspect these rooms without your stepfather knowing?”

“As it happens, he said he was coming to London today on important business. He will probably be away all day, so you should not be disturbed. We now have a housekeeper, but she is old and foolish. I could easily arrange for her to be elsewhere.”
“Excellent. You have no objection to the journey, Watson?”
“None at all.”
“Then we will both come. What are your own plans?”
“Since I am in town, there are one or two things I should like to do. But I will take the noon train home, so I shall be there when you arrive.”
“Expect us early this afternoon. I also have a little business to attend to. Will you stay for breakfast?”
“No, I must leave. Confiding my troubles to you has already eased my heart. I shall look forward to seeing you this afternoon.” She lowered her heavy black veil and slipped from the room.
“Well, Watson, what do you make of it?” Sherlock Holmes asked, leaning back in his chair.
“It strikes me as a very dark and sinister affair.”
“Dark and sinister enough, certainly.”
“Yet if she is right about the solid floor and walls, and if nobody could pass through the door, window, or chimney, her sister must have been alone when she met that mysterious death.”
“Then how do you account for the whistles at night, and those extraordinary words from the dying woman?”
“I have no idea.”

“Consider together the whistles at night, the gipsy band’s close friendship with the Doctor, and our strong reasons for believing he has an interest in preventing his stepdaughter’s marriage. Add the dying reference to a band, and finally the metallic clang Helen Stoner heard. One of the iron bars fastening the shutters might have made that noise as it fell into place. Taken together, these points suggest we may solve the mystery by following that line.”
“But what part did the gipsies play?”
“I cannot yet imagine.”
“I can see many difficulties with that theory.”
“So can I. That is exactly why we are going to Stoke Moran today. I want to discover whether the objections destroy the theory or can be explained. But what in the name of the devil—!”

My friend’s exclamation was prompted by our door flying open and a huge man filling the doorway. His clothes oddly combined a professional gentleman’s dress with a countryman’s: black top hat, long frock-coat, high gaiters, and a hunting-crop swinging in his hand. His hat brushed the top of the doorway, and his shoulders seemed to fill it from side to side. He turned his broad face from one of us to the other. Deep wrinkles scored it, the sun had burned it yellow, and every vicious passion appeared stamped upon it. His deep-set eyes with yellowed whites and high, thin, fleshless nose made him resemble some fierce old bird of prey.
“Which of you is Holmes?” this formidable figure demanded.
“That is my name, sir. But I do not know yours,” my companion answered calmly.
“I am Dr. Grimesby Roylott of Stoke Moran.”
“Indeed, Doctor,” Holmes replied pleasantly. “Please sit down.”
“I shall do no such thing. My stepdaughter came here. I followed her. What has she been telling you?”
“The weather is rather cold for this time of year,” Holmes observed.
“What has she told you?” the old man screamed in fury.
“Though I hear the crocuses are looking promising,” my companion continued, entirely untroubled.
“Ha! Trying to put me off?” The visitor stepped forward, shaking his hunting-crop. “I know you, you scoundrel! I have heard of you before. Holmes the meddler!”
My companion smiled.
“Holmes the busybody!”
The smile grew wider.
“Holmes, that puffed-up Scotland Yard official!”
Holmes gave a hearty chuckle. “Your conversation is delightful,” he said. “Please close the door when you leave. There is quite a draught.”

“I will leave when I am finished. Do not dare interfere in my affairs. I know Miss Stoner has been here. I followed her! I am a dangerous man to cross! Look at this.” He stepped quickly forward, grasped the poker, and bent it into a curve between his enormous brown hands.
“Keep clear of my hands,” he snarled. He flung the bent poker into the fireplace and strode out of the room.

“What a pleasant gentleman,” Holmes said, laughing. “I am not quite his size, but had he stayed, I might have shown him that my grip is scarcely weaker.” He picked up the steel poker and, with one sharp effort, pulled it straight again.

“Imagine the impudence of confusing me with the official detectives! Still, this encounter adds spice to our investigation. I only hope our little friend will not suffer for being careless enough to let that brute follow her. Now, Watson, let us order breakfast. Afterwards I shall walk to Doctors’ Commons, where I hope to find some useful information.”
Sherlock Holmes returned from his excursion at nearly one o’clock, carrying a sheet of blue paper covered with scribbled notes and figures.

“I have examined his late wife’s will,” he said. “To establish its precise effect, I had to calculate the present value of the investments involved. At her death they produced nearly eleven hundred pounds a year. Falling agricultural prices have reduced that to no more than seven hundred and fifty. On marriage, each daughter is entitled to two hundred and fifty pounds annually. Clearly, if both married, this fine gentleman would be left with a pittance. Even one marriage would seriously reduce his means. My morning has been worthwhile: it establishes the strongest possible motive for stopping either wedding. Now, Watson, this is too grave a matter for delay, especially since the old man knows we are looking into his affairs. If you are ready, let us take a cab to Waterloo. I should be grateful if you slipped your revolver into your pocket. An Eley’s No. 2 is a persuasive argument with gentlemen who can bend steel pokers into knots. That and a toothbrush should be all we need.”

At Waterloo we were fortunate enough to catch a train to Leatherhead. There we hired a carriage from the station inn and drove four or five miles through Surrey’s lovely lanes. The day was perfect: bright sunshine, a few fleecy clouds, and the first green shoots appearing on trees and roadside hedges. The pleasant scent of damp earth filled the air. To me, at least, spring’s gentle promise contrasted strangely with our sinister errand. Holmes sat at the front of the carriage, arms folded, hat low over his eyes, chin on his chest, buried deep in his own thoughts. Suddenly he stirred, tapped my shoulder, and pointed across the meadows.
“Look over there!” he said.
A well-wooded park rose gently towards a thicker grove on the crest. Through its branches appeared the grey gables and high roof ridge of a very old mansion.
“Is that Stoke Moran?” he asked.
“Yes, sir. That’s Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s house,” the driver replied.
“I see building work is under way,” Holmes said. “That is our destination.”

“The village is over there,” the driver said, pointing to roofs some distance to the left. “But for the house, it’s quicker to cross this stile and take the footpath through the fields. There’s the path, where that lady’s walking.”
“And I believe the lady is Miss Stoner,” Holmes said, shading his eyes. “Yes, we should take your advice.”
We climbed down and paid, and the carriage rattled away towards Leatherhead.

“I thought it best,” Holmes said as we crossed the stile, “to let him suppose we were architects, or here on some specific business. That may discourage gossip. Good afternoon, Miss Stoner. As you see, we have kept our promise.”

Our morning’s visitor hurried to meet us, delight clear on her face. “I have been waiting so eagerly for you!” she cried, shaking our hands warmly. “Everything has gone wonderfully. Dr. Roylott is in London and probably will not return before evening.”
“We have had the pleasure of meeting the Doctor,” Holmes said, briefly describing what had happened. As she listened, Miss Stoner turned pale to the lips.
“Good heavens!” she cried. “Then he followed me!”
“Apparently he did.”
“He is so cunning that I never know when I am safe. What will he say when he comes back?”

“He should beware: he may find someone even more cunning following his trail. Lock yourself away from him tonight. If he becomes violent, we will take you to your aunt in Harrow. Now we must use our time well. Please lead us straight to the rooms we need to inspect.”

The house was built of grey stone mottled with lichen, with a tall central block and two wings curving outward like a crab’s claws. One wing was a ruin: its windows broken and boarded, its roof partly collapsed. The centre was little better. The right-hand wing, however, was comparatively recent, and blinds at the windows and blue smoke rising from its chimneys showed where the family lived. Scaffolding stood against the end wall, where the masonry had been opened up, but there were no workmen to be seen when we arrived. Holmes paced slowly across the untidy lawn, studying the windows from outside with intense attention.
“This is the window of your former bedroom, I take it. The middle one was your sister’s, and the one nearest the main house is Dr. Roylott’s?”
“Exactly. But at present I occupy the middle bedroom.”
“While the alterations continue, I understand. Incidentally, I can see no urgent reason for repairs to that end wall.”
“There was no need at all. I believe it was a pretext to move me out of my room.”
“Ah! Significant. Along the opposite side of this narrow wing runs the corridor onto which the three rooms open. Does it have windows?”
“Yes, tiny ones. They are too narrow for anyone to get through.”
“Since you both locked your doors at night, nobody could enter from that side. Would you now go into your bedroom and fasten the shutters?”

She did so. After carefully inspecting through the open window, Holmes tried every possible way of forcing the shutter, without success. There was no gap where a knife could slip through to lift the bar. He examined the hinges with his lens, but they were solid iron, firmly embedded in thick masonry. “Hmm!” he said, rubbing his chin, plainly puzzled. “There certainly are difficulties with my theory. Nobody could get past those shutters while they were bolted. Let us see whether the interior sheds any light.”

A small side entrance opened into the whitewashed corridor serving the three bedrooms. Holmes declined to inspect the third, so we went directly to the middle room, where Miss Stoner now slept and where her sister had died. It was a simple little bedroom, low-ceilinged, with the wide fireplace usual in old country houses. In one corner stood a brown chest of drawers; in another, a narrow bed with a white counterpane. A dressing-table stood left of the window. Apart from two small wicker chairs and a square of Wilton carpet in the centre, that was everything. The exposed floorboards and wall panels were brown, worm-eaten oak, so ancient and discoloured that they might have been installed when the house was built. Holmes moved a chair into a corner and sat without speaking. His eyes roamed around the room, up and down, registering every detail.
“Where does that bell ring?” he finally asked, pointing to a thick bell-rope beside the bed. Its tassel rested on the pillow.
“It rings in the housekeeper’s room.”
“It seems newer than everything else here?”
“Yes. It was installed only a couple of years ago.”
“At your sister’s request, I suppose?”
“No. I never knew her to use it. We always fetched whatever we needed ourselves.”

“Indeed, such a fine bell-pull seems unnecessary here. Excuse me while I take a closer look at the floor.” With his lens in hand, he dropped onto his stomach and crawled quickly back and forth, inspecting every crack between the boards. Next he examined the wooden panelling just as closely. Then he walked across to the bed, studying it for some time and looking up and down the wall. Finally he grasped the bell-rope and gave it a sharp pull.
“Why, it is a sham,” he said.
“Does it not ring?”
“No. There is not even a wire connected to it. Most interesting. You can see it is tied to a hook just above that small ventilator opening.”
“How ridiculous! I had never noticed that.”

“Very strange!” Holmes muttered, tugging the rope. “Several things about this room are most unusual. What foolish builder, for instance, would put a ventilator into the next room when the same effort could have made an opening to the fresh air outside?”
“That is a recent addition too,” she said.
“Installed at the same time as the bell-rope?” Holmes asked.
“Yes. Several small alterations were made around that time.”
“Remarkable alterations: false bell-pulls and ventilators that provide no ventilation. With your permission, Miss Stoner, we shall extend our investigation to the room beyond.”

Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s bedroom was larger than his stepdaughter’s, though equally plain. Its main furnishings were a camp bed, a small wooden shelf filled mostly with technical books, an armchair beside the bed, a plain wooden chair against the wall, a round table, and a large iron safe. Holmes moved slowly about, examining each object with the closest interest.
“What does this hold?” he asked, tapping the safe.
“My stepfather keeps his business papers there.”
“Oh! So you have looked inside?”
“Once only, several years ago. I remember seeing it full of papers.”
“There is no cat inside, for instance?”
“No. What an extraordinary thought!”
“Then look at this!” He lifted a small saucer containing milk from the top of the safe.
“No, we have no cat. But we do have the cheetah and baboon.”

“Ah, naturally! A cheetah is a large cat, of course, though I doubt a saucer of milk would satisfy much of its appetite. There is one detail I want to establish.” He crouched before the wooden chair and studied its wooden seat with intense attention.
“Thank you. That settles the point,” he said, standing and pocketing his lens. “Hello! Here is something worth noticing!”
He had spotted a small dog whip hanging from a corner of the bed. Its lash had been doubled back and tied, forming a loop of whipcord.
“What do you think of that, Watson?”
“An ordinary enough whip. But I cannot explain why someone has tied it that way.”

“That part is less ordinary, is it not? Ah, what a wicked world! And when an intelligent man uses his brains for crime, it is worst of all. I think I have seen enough, Miss Stoner. If you agree, let us go onto the lawn.”

I had never seen my friend look so grim, or his brow so troubled, as when we left those rooms. We walked up and down the lawn several times. Neither Miss Stoner nor I wished to interrupt his thoughts. At last he emerged from his reverie.
“Miss Stoner,” he said, “you must follow every part of my advice exactly. It is absolutely essential.”
“I most certainly shall do so.”
“This is too serious for hesitation. Your life may depend on doing as I say.”
“You may be sure I shall do whatever you ask.”
“First of all, my friend and I must spend tonight in your bedroom.”
Miss Stoner and I both stared at him in amazement.
“Yes, it is necessary. Let me explain. That is the village inn over there, I believe?”
“Yes, the Crown Inn.”
“Good. Can your windows be seen from there?”
“Certainly.”

“When your stepfather returns, say you have a headache and stay in your room. Once you hear him retire for the night, open your shutters, unfasten the window catch, and put your lamp in the window to signal us. Then quietly take everything you may need back to your former bedroom. I am sure you can manage there for one night despite the repairs.”
“Oh, yes, quite easily.”
“You can leave everything else to us.”
“But what do you intend to do?”
“We shall remain in your room overnight and investigate the cause of the noise that has disturbed you.”
“Mr. Holmes, I believe you have already reached a conclusion,” Miss Stoner said, placing a hand on his sleeve.
“Perhaps I have done so.”
“Then, for pity’s sake, tell me exactly what killed my sister.”
“I would rather have clearer evidence before I say.”
“At least tell me whether I am right to think that a sudden fright killed her.”

“No, I do not believe so. I suspect a more tangible cause. Now we must leave, Miss Stoner. If Dr. Roylott comes back and sees us, our journey will have been wasted. Goodbye, and take courage. Follow my instructions, and you may be confident that we shall soon remove the dangers threatening you.”

Sherlock Holmes and I had no difficulty obtaining a bedroom and sitting-room upstairs at the Crown Inn. Our window overlooked the avenue gate and the occupied wing of Stoke Moran. At dusk we watched Dr. Roylott drive past, his enormous figure towering beside the boy who held the reins. The lad struggled a little with the heavy iron gates. We heard the Doctor’s hoarse roar and saw him shake clenched fists furiously at the boy. The carriage continued up the drive. A few minutes later a light appeared among the trees as someone lit a lamp in one of the sitting-rooms.
“Watson,” Holmes said as we sat in the deepening darkness, “I have some misgivings about taking you tonight. There is a definite risk of danger.”
“Can I be of any help?”
“Your presence could be invaluable.”
“Then I shall certainly go with you.”
“That is very kind of you.”
“You mention danger. Plainly you noticed things in those rooms that I did not see.”
“No. I suspect I merely drew more conclusions. I imagine you saw everything that I saw.”
“Only the bell-rope struck me as unusual, and I confess I cannot imagine what purpose it serves.”
“You noticed the ventilator as well?”
“Yes, but a small opening between two rooms is hardly anything extraordinary. This one was so tiny that even a rat would scarcely fit through it.”
“Before we ever reached Stoke Moran, I knew we would find a ventilator.”
“My dear Holmes!”

“Yes, I did. Remember what she told us in her account: her sister could smell Dr. Roylott’s cigar. That immediately suggested that there must be an opening between the rooms. It must be small, or the coroner’s enquiry would have mentioned it. So I inferred a ventilator.”
“But what could be harmful about that?”
“At the very least, the timing is curious. A ventilator is installed, a rope hung, and the woman sleeping in that bed dies. Does that not strike you?”
“I still cannot see how they connect.”
“Did you notice anything particularly odd about the bed?”
“No.”
“It was fixed to the floor. Have you ever seen a bed secured like that?”
“I cannot say I ever have.”
“She could not move it. The bed must always stay in precisely the same position relative to the ventilator and the rope. We should call it a rope, since it was clearly never intended to ring a bell.”
“Holmes!” I cried. “I begin to glimpse what you mean. We have arrived only just in time to prevent a cunning and dreadful crime.”

“Cunning and dreadful indeed. A doctor who turns criminal is the most dangerous of all: he has both courage and knowledge. Palmer and Pritchard were leaders in their profession. This man goes deeper still, but I believe we can go deeper than he does, Watson. We shall face enough horrors before the night ends. For heaven’s sake, let us smoke quietly and think about something more cheerful for a few hours.”

At about nine the light among the trees went out, leaving the manor-house in darkness. Two long hours slowly crept past. Then, exactly as eleven struck, one bright light suddenly appeared directly ahead of us.
“Our signal,” Holmes said, springing up. “It is in the middle window.”

As we went out, he exchanged a few words with the landlord, explaining that we were making a late call on an acquaintance and might stay the night there. Moments later we were on the dark road, a cold wind in our faces. Ahead, a single yellow light gleamed through the gloom, guiding us towards our sombre errand.

Entering the grounds was easy: unrepaired gaps yawned in the old boundary wall. We threaded our way between the trees, reached the lawn, and crossed it. Just as we were about to climb through the window, something like a hideously misshapen child burst from a clump of laurels. It flung itself onto the grass, limbs twisting, then ran swiftly across the lawn into the dark.
“My God!” I whispered. “Did you see that?”
For an instant Holmes was as startled as I was. In his alarm his hand gripped my wrist like a vice. Then he laughed softly and brought his lips close to my ear.
“A pleasant household,” he murmured. “That was the baboon.”

I had forgotten the Doctor’s peculiar pets. There was a cheetah too; it might leap onto our shoulders at any moment. I admit I was relieved when, after following Holmes’s example and removing my shoes, I found myself inside the bedroom. Silently he shut the shutters, moved the lamp to the table, and surveyed the room. Everything remained as we had seen it that afternoon. He then crept close and cupped a hand around his mouth. His next whisper was so faint that I could scarcely make out the words:
“The slightest noise would ruin our plan.”
I nodded to indicate that I understood.
“We must remain in darkness. He could see a light through the ventilator.”
Once more I nodded.
“Stay awake. Your life may depend on it. Keep your pistol ready in case it is needed. I shall sit on the edge of the bed; take that chair.”
I drew my revolver and placed it at the table’s corner.
Holmes had brought a long, slender cane, which he set on the bed beside him. Next to it he put a matchbox and a candle end. He then turned down the lamp, leaving us in darkness.

How could I ever forget that terrible watch? No sound reached me, not even the drawing of a breath. Yet I knew my friend sat only a few feet away, wide awake and as tense as I was. The shutters excluded every trace of light. We waited in complete darkness.

Occasionally a night bird called outside. Once, just beyond our window, a long, catlike whine confirmed that the cheetah was roaming free. Far away, the parish clock sounded its deep notes at every quarter of an hour. How slowly those quarters passed! Midnight struck, then one, two, and three. Still we sat silently, waiting for whatever might come.

Suddenly a brief flash appeared near the ventilator and vanished at once. A strong smell of burning oil and hot metal followed: someone had lit a shuttered lantern in the next room. I heard a slight movement, then silence returned, though the smell intensified. For half an hour I listened with straining ears. Then another sound emerged, faint and soothing, like a thin, continuous jet of steam escaping from a kettle. The instant we heard it, Holmes leaped from the bed, struck a match, and beat furiously at the bell-rope with his cane.
“Do you see it, Watson?” he shouted. “Do you see it?”

I saw nothing. As Holmes struck the match, I heard a low, clear whistle. But the sudden flare dazzled my tired eyes, and I could not distinguish the thing he was striking so violently. I could see, however, that his face had gone deathly pale with horror and disgust. He stopped striking and stared towards the ventilator. Then the night’s silence broke with the most appalling cry I have ever heard. It grew louder and louder, a hoarse scream mingling pain, terror, and rage. They say it woke people in the village and even at the distant parsonage, bringing them out of their beds. Our hearts chilled. I stood staring at Holmes, and he at me, until the last echoes faded into the silence from which they had arisen.
“What does it mean?” I gasped.
“It means the affair is over,” Holmes replied. “Perhaps that is best, after all. Bring your pistol. We shall go into Dr. Roylott’s room.”

Solemnly he lit the lamp and led me along the corridor. He knocked twice at the bedroom door without receiving an answer. Then he turned the handle and entered. I followed directly behind, my cocked pistol in my hand.

An extraordinary scene confronted us. On the table stood a shuttered lantern, half open, casting a brilliant beam onto the iron safe, whose door was ajar. Beside the table, in the wooden chair, sat Dr. Grimesby Roylott. His long grey dressing-gown left his ankles bare above red, backless Turkish slippers. Across his lap lay the short-handled whip with the long lash that we had seen earlier. His chin pointed upwards and his eyes stared horribly, rigidly, at a corner of the ceiling. A strange yellow band with brownish speckles seemed wound tightly around his forehead. He neither moved nor spoke as we came in.
“The band! The speckled band!” Holmes whispered.
